dogon_yeban.name: Dwell as the hidden earth-genies of the underworld
dogon_yeban.notes: The Yeban are misshapen subterranean genies who inhabit the holes and caves of the earth, born of Ogo the Pale Fox's incest with the earth.

sources.reference: Griaule & Dieterlen, Le Renard pâle (1965)

dogon_yeban.name: Engender and instruct the Andoumboulou
dogon_yeban.notes: The Yeban engendered the Andoumboulou, the small first humanoids who learned speech and craft from them.

sources.reference: Griaule, Conversations with Ogotemmêli (1965)

e_bangishimog.name: Govern the West and rule as Father of the Winds
e_bangishimog.notes: The mighty West Wind manidoo, ruler of the land of the west (Bangishimog) and father of the four winds in Anishinaabe cosmology.

sources.reference: Schoolcraft, Algic Researches (1839)

e_bangishimog.name: Sire Nanabozho and his brothers upon a mortal woman
e_bangishimog.notes: By the mortal Wiininwaa he fathered the culture-hero Wenabozho (Nanabozho), the wolf Ma'iingan and their brothers.

sources.reference: Schoolcraft, Algic Researches (1839)

edo_esu.name: Govern crossroads, chance and the traffic between worlds
edo_esu.notes: Adopted from the Yoruba Eshu, the Edo Esu rules junctions, lots and the unpredictable, mediating fortune and misfortune.

sources.reference: R. E. Bradbury, The Benin Kingdom and the Edo-Speaking Peoples (1957)

edo_olokun.name: Bestow purity, peace and cleansing through white chalk
edo_olokun.notes: Olokun's worship centres on orhue (riverside kaolin chalk), the Edo emblem of purity, joy and peace used in his rites of cleansing.

sources.reference: Bradbury, The Benin Kingdom and the Edo-Speaking Peoples (1957)

edo_ogiuwu.name: Dispense death as the youngest child of Osanobua
edo_ogiuwu.notes: In the creation account Osanobua assigned Ogiuwu the office of dispenser of death, claiming the lives of mortals at their appointed end.

sources.reference: Bradbury, The Benin Kingdom and the Edo-Speaking Peoples (1957)

egyptian_amenmesse.name: Seize Thebes and rule Upper Egypt and Kush as rival king
egyptian_amenmesse.notes: During Seti II's reign Amenmesse took control of Thebes, Upper Egypt and Nubia, ruling the south as a rival pharaoh before his defeat.

sources.reference: Dodson, Poisoned Legacy: The Decline and Fall of the Nineteenth Egyptian Dynasty (2010)

egyptian_amunherkhepeshef.name: Serve as crown prince and army commander at his father's side
egyptian_amunherkhepeshef.notes: Firstborn of Ramesses II and heir apparent; depicted as a young commander in the Battle of Kadesh reliefs, the template of Ramesside crown-prince martial iconography.

sources.reference: Kadesh reliefs of Ramesses II (Abu Simbel, Ramesseum, Luxor)

egyptian_merneptah.name: Repel the Libyan and Sea-Peoples invasion at Perire
egyptian_merneptah.notes: In year 5 (c. 1208 BCE) defeated the combined Libyan and Sea-Peoples coalition, commemorated on the Merneptah Stele.

sources.reference: Merneptah Stele (Cairo Museum JE 31408)

egyptian_merneptah.name: Reign as the living Horus, son of Ramesses II
egyptian_merneptah.notes: Acceded at advanced age as the thirteenth son after the deaths of his elder brothers, embodying pharaonic kingship as the living Horus.

sources.reference: Merneptah Stele (Cairo Museum JE 31408)

egyptian_horus.name: Embody pharaonic kingship as the living king
egyptian_horus.notes: From Dynasty 0 the reigning pharaoh IS Horus, identified by the Horus-name of the royal titulary.

sources.reference: Pyramid Texts; Egyptian royal Horus-name titulary

egyptian_horus.name: Avenge Osiris and win the kingship from Set
egyptian_horus.notes: In the Contendings of Horus and Set he overcomes his uncle to claim his father's throne, the founding legitimation narrative of Egyptian kingship.

sources.reference: Contendings of Horus and Seth (Papyrus Chester Beatty I)

egyptian_horus.name: Hold the sun and moon as his two eyes across the sky
egyptian_horus.notes: As Horus-of-the-Two-Horizons (Harakhty) the falcon's eyes are sun and moon; the moon-eye is wounded by Set and healed (the wedjat).

sources.reference: Pyramid Texts; Coffin Texts

egyptian_atum.name: Descend as the evening sun returning to the primeval waters
egyptian_atum.notes: Atum is the aged setting sun that re-enters Nun each night, complement to the rising Khepri and midday Ra.

sources.reference: Pyramid Texts; Coffin Texts

egyptian_bastet.name: Embody the gentle, pacified Eye of Ra
egyptian_bastet.notes: The benign cat-form counterpart to the raging lioness Sekhmet, soothing the solar Eye's wrath.

sources.reference: Coffin Texts; temple of Bubastis

egyptian_bastet.name: Nurse and protect the king as the lioness-mother
egyptian_bastet.notes: In her fiercer aspect she defends the king and nurses him, a protective lioness against enemies.

sources.reference: Wilkinson, The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt (2003)

egyptian_bes.name: Guard mother and child through labour and infancy
egyptian_bes.notes: Bes attends the birthing-bower, frightening off hostile spirits that threaten the mother and newborn.

sources.reference: Pinch, Magic in Ancient Egypt (1994)

egyptian_bes.name: Bring music, dance and merriment into the home
egyptian_bes.notes: A god of revelry and apotropaic joy, depicted with drums, tambourines and dancing.

sources.reference: Wilkinson, The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt (2003)

egyptian_geb.name: Hold the dead and the seeds within his earthly body
egyptian_geb.notes: As the earth itself Geb both imprisons the dead in his soil and yields vegetation and grain.

sources.reference: Pyramid Texts; Coffin Texts

egyptian_hapi.name: Bind together Upper and Lower Egypt at the throne
egyptian_hapi.notes: Twin Hapi figures perform the sema-tawy, knotting papyrus and lotus around the royal throne to unite the Two Lands.

sources.reference: Sema-tawy throne-side reliefs (e.g. Karnak, royal statuary)

egyptian_hathor.name: Suckle and nourish the king as the divine cow
egyptian_hathor.notes: As the celestial cow Hathor suckles the pharaoh, conferring divine sustenance and legitimacy.

sources.reference: Wilkinson, The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt (2003)

egyptian_hathor.name: Be pacified through music, dance and drunkenness
egyptian_hathor.notes: In the myth of the Distant Goddess the raging Eye is appeased and returns as joyful Hathor, celebrated with the Festival of Drunkenness.

sources.reference: Myth of the Heavenly Cow; Dendera temple texts

egyptian_heka.name: Empower the gods and the act of creation itself
egyptian_heka.notes: Heka is the primal creative force present before duality, by which the creator and all gods accomplish their works.

sources.reference: Coffin Texts spell 261

egyptian_heka.name: Sustain and protect the sun-god in his barque
egyptian_heka.notes: Personified Heka travels in the solar barque, his magic warding the sun-god through the day and the underworld.

sources.reference: Coffin Texts; Book of the Dead

egyptian_khonsu.name: Measure and define time as the traveller of the night sky
egyptian_khonsu.notes: As 'Khonsu the Wanderer' the moon-god marks the months and the passage of time.

sources.reference: Wilkinson, The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt (2003)

egyptian_min.name: Renew the king's potency and guarantee the harvest
egyptian_min.notes: In the Coming-Forth-of-Min festival the king cuts the first sheaf and the god's restored virility ensures fertile fields.

sources.reference: Festival reliefs, Medinet Habu (temple of Ramesses III)

egyptian_min.name: Protect the eastern-desert roads and mining expeditions
egyptian_min.notes: As Lord of the Eastern Desert Min watched over the Coptos caravan routes to the Red Sea and the desert quarries.

sources.reference: Wilkinson, The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt (2003)

egyptian_mut.name: Mother the gods and the king as the Theban great mother
egyptian_mut.notes: As 'Mut the Mother' she bears and protects the king and the divine child Khonsu of the Theban Triad.

sources.reference: Wilkinson, The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt (2003)

egyptian_neith.name: Guard the dead and the canopic viscera with Selket and her sisters
egyptian_neith.notes: One of the four tutelary goddesses of the canopic shrine, Neith protects the deceased (with the duamutef jar in particular).

sources.reference: Canopic shrine of Tutankhamun; Pyramid Texts

egyptian_nekhbet.name: Crown the king as the Two Ladies with Wadjet
egyptian_nekhbet.notes: Nekhbet of El-Kab (Upper Egypt) and Wadjet of Buto (Lower Egypt) form the nebty Two-Ladies title of the royal titulary.

sources.reference: Egyptian royal nebty (Two Ladies) titulary

egyptian_anubis.name: Guide and escort the dead through the necropolis
egyptian_anubis.notes: As 'Foremost of the Westerners' (an early role later given to Osiris) Anubis leads the deceased to judgment.

sources.reference: Pyramid Texts; Book of the Dead

edo_olokun.name: Olokun worship and initiation
edo_olokun.notes: Local congregations, drawn especially from women seeking children, pray and sacrifice to Olokun; mud-shrine figures and waterpots, coral-bead regalia and orhue chalk feature in fourteen-day initiation and purification rites.

sources.reference: Ben-Amos, The Art of Benin (1995); Bradbury (1957)

egyptian_bastet.name: Feast of Bubastis
egyptian_bastet.notes: Herodotus describes a vast river-procession festival at Bubastis with music, dancing and wine, drawing crowds from across Egypt; votive bronze cats and mummified cats were dedicated.

sources.reference: Herodotus, Histories 2.59-60

egyptian_min.name: Coming Forth of Min (Procession of Min)
egyptian_min.notes: Harvest festival in which the cult-image was carried to the fields, the king cut the first sheaf of grain, and games (including pole-climbing) were held; well attested at Medinet Habu.

sources.reference: Festival reliefs, Medinet Habu (temple of Ramesses III)

egyptian_imhotep.name: Cult of Imhotep, son of Ptah
egyptian_imhotep.notes: Deified in the Late Period as a healing god; pilgrims sought cures and incubation dreams at sanctuaries, especially at Saqqara, Memphis (Asklepieion) and Philae, where he was syncretized with Asklepios.

sources.reference: Wildung, Imhotep und Amenhotep (1977)

egyptian_amun.name: Opet Festival
egyptian_amun.notes: Annual Theban procession in which Amun's cult-image travelled by barque from Karnak to Luxor Temple to renew the king's ka and divine kingship.

sources.reference: Opet reliefs, Luxor Temple colonnade

egyptian_khonsu.name: Cult of Khonsu the Merciful at Karnak
egyptian_khonsu.notes: As Khonsu-pa-ir-sekher ('who works destiny/expels demons') he was sought for healing and exorcism; the Bentresh Stela recounts his image sent abroad to cure a foreign princess.

sources.reference: Bentresh Stela (Louvre C 284)

egyptian_hathor.name: Festival of Drunkenness
egyptian_hathor.notes: Celebrated the pacified return of the raging Eye as joyful Hathor through music, dance and ritual intoxication, prominently at Dendera and Mut's precinct.

sources.reference: Dendera temple texts; Mut precinct, Karnak

attributes.name: Amphibious, fish-tailed serpentine body
attributes.notes: The Nommo are depicted as half-human, half-fish (or serpent) water beings, often raising their arms in the gesture of the binu masters of water.

sources.reference: Griaule & Dieterlen, Le Renard pâle (1965)
Griaule, Conversations with Ogotemmêli (1965)

attributes.name: Footprints read in the divination sand-grid
attributes.notes: Ogo the Pale Fox is known by the tracks he leaves overnight in the bait-strewn divination tables, which diviners read at dawn.

sources.reference: Griaule & Dieterlen, Le Renard pâle (1965)
Griaule & Dieterlen, Le Renard pâle (1965)

attributes.name: Human torso with mudfish legs and coral regalia
attributes.notes: Olokun is shown with a human upper body and mudfish for legs, crowned and draped in coral beads, holding the wealth of the deep.

sources.reference: Ben-Amos, The Art of Benin (1995)

attributes.name: Riverside white chalk (orhue) and waterpots
attributes.notes: Mud shrine-figures, waterpots and orhue kaolin chalk mark his altars as emblems of purity and the waters.

sources.reference: Bradbury, The Benin Kingdom and the Edo-Speaking Peoples (1957)
Ben-Amos, The Art of Benin (1995)
Ben-Amos, The Art of Benin (1995)

attributes.name: Black jackal head or recumbent black jackal
attributes.notes: Depicted as a man with a black canine head or as a recumbent jackal on a shrine; the black colour evokes both decay's reversal and the fertile silt of rebirth.

sources.reference: Wilkinson, The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt (2003)
Wilkinson, The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt (2003)

attributes.name: Woman with the head of a cat (earlier lioness)
attributes.notes: Shown as a cat-headed woman, often with kittens at her feet and a sistrum or basket in hand, the gentler counterpart of the lioness Sekhmet.

sources.reference: Herodotus, Histories 2.59-60
Herodotus, Histories 2.66-67

attributes.name: Frontal-faced bearded dwarf with leonine features and lolling tongue
attributes.notes: Uniquely shown full-face (not in profile), a grotesque protective dwarf with lion's mane, ears and tail, often wearing a plumed crown.

sources.reference: Wilkinson, The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt (2003)
Pinch, Magic in Ancient Egypt (1994)

attributes.name: Reclining green or black man beneath arched Nut
attributes.notes: Geb is shown lying beneath the sky-goddess Nut, his body green or black for vegetation and silt, sometimes ithyphallic, reaching up toward her.

sources.reference: Wilkinson, The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt (2003)
Wilkinson, The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt (2003)

attributes.name: Man with the head of a horizontally-horned ram
attributes.notes: Shown ram-headed, frequently seated at a potter's wheel modelling a child, lord of the Elephantine cataract.

sources.reference: Wilkinson, The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt (2003)
Wilkinson, The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt (2003)

attributes.name: Ithyphallic mummiform figure with raised flail and twin plumes
attributes.notes: Shown wrapped, with one arm raised holding a flail behind his tall double-plumed crown, and an erect phallus signalling fertility.

sources.reference: Wilkinson, The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt (2003)
Wilkinson, The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt (2003)

sacredPlants.name: Cos lettuce (Lactuca, for its milky aphrodisiac sap)

sources.reference: Wilkinson, The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt (2003)

attributes.name: Woman in a vulture headdress wearing the Double Crown
attributes.notes: Shown as a woman wearing the vulture cap surmounted by the Pschent, often with a long red or blue dress; in fierce aspect lioness-headed.

sources.reference: Wilkinson, The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt (2003)
Wilkinson, The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt (2003)

attributes.name: Woman wearing the Red Crown with bow and arrows
attributes.notes: Shown crowned with the Red Crown of Lower Egypt, sometimes bearing crossed arrows on a shield or a weaving shuttle.

sources.reference: Wilkinson, The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt (2003)

attributes.name: Vulture with outstretched protective wings holding shen-rings
attributes.notes: Shown as a griffon vulture hovering over the king, clutching shen-rings of eternity in her talons, or as a woman in the White Crown.

sources.reference: Wilkinson, The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt (2003)
Wilkinson, The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt (2003)

attributes.name: Mummiform youth with side-lock and lunar disk-in-crescent
attributes.notes: Shown as a tightly-wrapped young man wearing the side-lock of youth and a full-moon disk cradled in a crescent, holding crook and flail.

sources.reference: Wilkinson, The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt (2003)

attributes.name: Cow, or woman with cow-ears and horns enclosing a sun-disk
attributes.notes: Appears as a cow, a cow-eared woman, or a frontal Hathor-head capital, crowned with cow-horns and a solar disk.

sources.reference: Wilkinson, The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt (2003)
Wilkinson, The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt (2003)

sacredPlants.name: Sycomore fig (she is Lady of the Sycamore)

sources.reference: Wilkinson, The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt (2003)

attributes.name: Man in a tall twin-plumed (shuti) crown, skin often blue
attributes.notes: Shown as an enthroned man wearing the flat-topped double-plumed crown, frequently with blue (lapis) flesh marking his celestial, hidden nature.

sources.reference: Wilkinson, The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt (2003)
Karnak ram-headed sphinx avenue
Wilkinson, The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt (2003)

attributes.name: Falcon, or falcon-headed man in the Double Crown
attributes.notes: Shown as a falcon or a falcon-headed man wearing the Pschent; as Harpokrates a naked child with side-lock and finger to mouth.

sources.reference: Wilkinson, The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt (2003)
